description: The CBOR layer beneath the metrological one, exercised directly. Everything else in this project reaches the reader through a metrological entry point, so the reader is only ever asked about bytes that were already going to be a reading; these cases ask it about bytes that are not. A text string that is not UTF-8, and a document nested past any sensible bound, have to be refused by the reader itself rather than by anything above it. Both libraries validate strictly by default — C# through CBORUTF8Validation.Strict, TypeScript through a TextDecoder in fatal mode — and until now nothing checked that they draw the line in the same place. Read with each library’s DEFAULT reader options rather than a strict preset, because what is being compared is what a caller who asked for nothing in particular gets.

cases.reason: a text string MUST be valid UTF-8 (RFC 8949 §3.1)
cases.description: 0x80 is a continuation byte with no lead byte in front of it. The shortest possible invalid string, and the one a decoder that only checks lengths will let through.

cases.reason: a text string MUST be valid UTF-8 (RFC 8949 §3.1)
cases.description: 0xC3 announces a two-byte sequence and the string ends. Truncation inside a character, which is what a naive concatenation of two chunks produces.

cases.reason: a text string MUST be valid UTF-8 (RFC 8949 §3.1)
cases.description: Three bytes of a four-byte character. The CBOR length is honest about the three bytes, which is why a length check alone cannot catch it.

cases.reason: a text string MUST be valid UTF-8 (RFC 8949 §3.1); overlong forms are not UTF-8
cases.description: U+002F "/" written in two bytes instead of one. Decoders that accept overlong forms have been the mechanism of path-traversal filter bypasses for twenty years: the filter sees no slash, the consumer sees one.

cases.reason: a text string MUST be valid UTF-8 (RFC 8949 §3.1); surrogate code points are not encodable
cases.description: U+D800, a lone surrogate half. It is a legal UTF-16 code unit and not a legal UTF-8 character, so a library that converts by way of its host string type can leak one through without noticing.

cases.reason: a text string MUST be valid UTF-8 (RFC 8949 §3.1)
cases.description: 0xFE occurs nowhere in UTF-8, at any position.

cases.reason: a text string MUST be valid UTF-8 (RFC 8949 §3.1)
cases.description: 0xFF, likewise. Together with the previous case this is the byte-order-mark pair, which is what a UTF-16 document mistakenly labelled as CBOR text starts with.
"ä" - the control that says the rejections above are about validity rather than about anything non-ASCII.

U+1F600, a character outside the basic multilingual plane. A library working through UTF-16 internally holds this as a surrogate *pair*, which must come back out as four bytes and not as two three-byte sequences.
The empty text string. Nothing to validate, and the place an over-eager validator falls over.
One array around one integer. The floor: whatever the depth count means, this is inside it.
Half the default bound. Deeper than any real document and still comfortably admissible, so a disagreement here would be about the counting rule rather than about the limit.

cases.reason: beyond any reasonable nesting bound; a decoder MUST NOT recurse without limit
cases.description: Far past the bound on both sides. A decoder that accepts this recurses on attacker-controlled input, which is a stack overflow rather than a parse error - and a stack overflow is not catchable in either runtime.
One inside the default bound. Recorded rather than judged: where exactly the count starts is undocumented on both sides.
The default bound itself. Whether it is the last accepted depth or the first rejected one is the whole question this case exists to record.
One past the default bound. Together with the two above, these three say precisely where each library stops - which is what a maintainer needs before changing the number.
